children: Indian primary copper producers are seeking a reduction in GST from 18 per cent to 5 per cent, saying elevated copper prices are locking up working capital across the supply chain and raising financing pressures

India's primary copper producers are seeking a reduction in the Goods and Services Tax (GST) on a range of copper products from 18 per cent to 5 per cent, as record-high prices increase working-capital requirements across the supply chain.

The Indian Primary Copper Producers Association is in discussions with the government over the proposed tax reduction, its president Rohit Pathak said. According to the industry body, the move could unlock as much as USD 3.6 billion of capital currently tied up in tax payments.

The demand comes as copper prices have climbed to record levels globally. Copper crossed USD 14,700 a tonne on the London Metal Exchange this month, increasing the amount of capital required to finance purchases and maintain inventories.
Record Prices Increase Working Capital Needs
The impact is being felt across the copper value chain, including among primary producers and downstream manufacturers.

Pathak said primary producers purchasing feedstock for processing and downstream manufacturers buying copper products both bear the upfront tax burden. Higher copper prices consequently translate into a larger amount of working capital being tied up in GST payments.
Primary copper producers such as Hindalco Industries, which operates with a roughly three-month concentrate cycle, are also facing higher working-capital requirements, according to Pathak.

The association has argued that the current tax burden locks up capital that could otherwise be deployed towards expansion and investment. The domestic copper industry is currently undertaking a multibillion-dollar investment programme, Pathak said.
The sharp rise in copper prices is also changing inventory behaviour among cable manufacturers and dealers.
With stockpiling becoming more expensive, Indian cable makers and dealers have been reducing inventories, with stocks now being maintained for days rather than weeks, according to Pathak.
The development comes as higher metal prices increase the cost of carrying inventory and place additional pressure on businesses that need copper as a key manufacturing input.
Import Dependence Adds To Cost Pressure
The increase in copper prices is also adding to cost pressures in India, which has become more dependent on imports following the 2018 shutdown of Vedanta's Sterlite copper smelter.
The industry's GST demand therefore comes against a backdrop of elevated international prices, higher financing requirements and efforts by domestic producers to expand copper capacity.

For producers and downstream users, a reduction in GST would reduce the amount of capital tied up in the tax component of transactions, while potentially easing liquidity pressures across the copper supply chain.
